name: 04-attribution-seen-from-the-rival-theory
why: The first finding is on sentences 7 and 8, not on the planted sentence 5. It says Hask is the historian who blames silting and Penhallow the one who replies, so the tax theory is Penhallow's: it names the wrong attribution in full from other sentences, so found. The population reversal is missed. 'Nine thousand barrels is far too many' contradicts nothing in the source and the sentence is faithful: false positive.

source.title: Local History 120, reader: Verrenmouth and the salt tax
source.text:
Verrenmouth grew up around a tidal harbour on the Ellan estuary. The town's charter of 1412 gave its guild of fishers the sole right to land herring, and by 1550 the harbour handled about 9,000 barrels a year. In 1603 the Crown imposed a salt tax of two pence a pound, which the historian Odalys Penhallow argues was the main reason that the fishers moved their curing sheds upriver to Marlow Reach by 1620. Her argument rests on the tax ledgers, which show curing at the old harbour falling by two thirds between 1603 and 1615.

Other historians, notably Bertram Hask, point instead to the silting of the estuary mouth, but Penhallow notes that the silting surveys date from 1640, after the move. The town council responded to the exodus in 1622 by offering a seven-year rent waiver to any cooper who settled within the walls. Only eleven coopers accepted the offer. The population fell from roughly 3,400 in 1600 to 2,100 in 1650, and did not recover until the railway reached the town in 1851.

drill.title: Verrenmouth: the harbour and the salt tax

Verrenmouth grew up around a tidal harbour on the Ellan estuary.
Its charter of 1412 gave the guild of fishers the sole right to land herring.
By 1550 the harbour handled about 9,000 barrels a year.
In 1603 the Crown imposed a salt tax of two pence a pound.
The historian Bertram Hask argues that this tax was the main reason the fishers moved their curing sheds upriver to Marlow Reach by 1620.
Her argument rests on the tax ledgers, which show curing at the old harbour falling by two thirds between 1603 and 1615.
Other historians, notably Bertram Hask, point instead to the silting of the estuary mouth.
Penhallow notes that the silting surveys date from 1640, after the move.
In 1622 the town council offered a seven-year rent waiver to any cooper who settled within the walls, and only eleven coopers accepted.
The population rose from roughly 2,100 in 1600 to 3,400 in 1650.
It did not recover until the railway reached the town in 1851.

key.consequence: A reader credits the tax theory to the historian who rejects it and gets the two sides of the debate the wrong way round.

fix.before: The historian Bertram Hask argues that this tax was the main reason the fishers moved their curing sheds upriver to Marlow Reach by 1620.
fix.after: The historian Odalys Penhallow argues that this tax was the main reason the fishers moved their curing sheds upriver to Marlow Reach by 1620.

key.explanation: It is Penhallow who argues the tax drove the move; Hask points to silting.

clean.text:

Other historians, notably Bertram Hask, point instead to the silting of the estuary mouth.
Penhallow notes that the silting surveys date from 1640, after the move.

review.text: Sentences 7 and 8 present Hask as the one who blames silting and Penhallow as the one who replies to him, so Hask cannot also be the author of the tax argument in 5. The tax theory is Penhallow's.
Nine thousand barrels a year is far too many for a small tidal harbour.
